beats.say: You think Italy was just a Mediterranean kingdom, but in 1912 it secretly plotted a mountain alliance with Austria-Hungary.
The Alpine fortress at Fort Bard became the clandestine meeting point for generals plotting a joint offensive against France.
On June 15, 1912, General Luigi Cadorna signed a covert protocol promising Austrian troops passage through the Brenner Pass.
Venice's Arsenal stored extra artillery, hidden from the public eye, ready to be shipped north under the cover of a trade convoy.
Meanwhile, Rome's foreign ministry whispered to Berlin, leveraging the secret pact to pressure France over the Tunisian crisis.
The plan hinged on a swift victory in Libya, believing a quick win would buy diplomatic leverage in the Balkans.
But the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Lule Burgas in November 1912 shattered any hope of coordinated action.
News of the secret Alpine pact leaked to the press, forcing Victor Emmanuel III to publicly deny any alliance.
The scandal crippled Italy's credibility, contributing to the internal dissent that sparked the 1914 military mutinies.
History remembers the Italo-Turkish war, yet this hidden Alpine pact reveals Italy's deeper ambitions before World I.
